title: Piano Concerto No. 3 in C major
hook: A concerto that sparkles, jokes and argues, written by a pianist for his own hands.

painting.title: Breton Girls Dancing, Pont-Aven
painting.pairingNote: A round dance in a Brittany hayfield; Prokofiev finished the concerto on the Brittany coast in the summer of 1921, and much of it dances.

facts: Prokofiev was one of the great pianists of his time, and he wrote this concerto to play himself. It is the most popular of his five piano concertos.

It grew slowly. He wrote the theme of the second movement in 1913 and gathered more ideas over the next years, in Russia. He left Russia in 1918, and in the summer of 1921, staying on the coast of Brittany in France, he finally put the concerto together.

He played the first performance on 16 December 1921 in Chicago, with the Chicago Symphony Orchestra conducted by Frederick Stock. Success came a year later, after a much-praised performance in Paris conducted by Serge Koussevitzky.
The piano part is famously hard: fast runs, hammered chords, leaps across the keyboard. But the concerto is also full of tunes and jokes, and the orchestra is a real partner.
bigPicture.inOneLine: a dreamy clarinet that launches a race (I), a theme with five very different variations (II), an argument between piano and orchestra that ends in a blaze of C major (III).

movements.heading: Andante – Allegro
movements.summary: A quiet, folk-like melody on a solo clarinet, then a sudden race. The piano bursts in with brilliant, fast music, and a second theme brings a spiky, mocking dance. In the middle the clarinet’s slow melody returns in the full orchestra; then the race starts again and drives to the end.

mainIdeas.name: The opening song
mainIdeas.description: a calm, Russian-sounding melody on a solo clarinet.

mainIdeas.name: The race
mainIdeas.description: fast, glittering runs in the piano, with the strings rushing alongside.

mainIdeas.name: The mocking dance
mainIdeas.description: a spiky, sardonic tune, first in the oboe, then in the piano, with castanets.

stops.hear: A solo clarinet, alone, plays a calm, gentle melody
The strings suddenly rush forward in fast notes
The piano bursts in with brilliant, racing runs
stops.happening: The piano’s entry, with the first theme

stops.hear: A spiky, mocking tune in the oboe; the piano takes it up, with castanets clicking
The piano hammers out fast octaves and clashing chords
The orchestra plays the clarinet’s slow melody, now broad and loud; the piano weaves delicate patterns around it
stops.happening: The opening song returns, in the middle of the movement

stops.hear: The race starts again: piano and strings rush off together
The mocking tune returns in the piano
Faster and louder; piano and orchestra drive towards the end

stops.label: Last 15 seconds
stops.hear: A sudden stop on bare, open octaves
stops.happening: An abrupt, almost bare ending in C

notice: Compare the clarinet’s melody at the start with its return at about four minutes. Same tune, completely different force.
In the fast music, the piano rarely has a long melody. Its job is energy: runs, leaps and hammered chords.

notes.title: In this recording
notes.body: Martha Argerich was in her mid-twenties when she recorded the concerto with Claudio Abbado in Berlin in 1967. On the Spotify album it is tracks 1–3, followed by Ravel’s Concerto in G from the same sessions.

movements.heading: Tema con variazioni
movements.summary: A short, elegant theme in the rhythm of an old dance, the gavotte, followed by five [[variation|variation]]s, each with its own character: dreamy, galloping, jazzy, mysterious and fierce. At the end the theme returns in the orchestra while the piano races around it, and the movement fades out quietly.

mainIdeas.name: The theme
mainIdeas.description: a poised, slightly ironic melody in the woodwinds, in the steps of a gavotte.

mainIdeas.name: The variations
mainIdeas.description: the same theme, transformed each time.

stops.hear: The orchestra alone: a poised, graceful melody in the woodwinds, with soft strings
The piano enters with a long [[trill|trill]], then plays the theme slowly and dreamily
Suddenly fast: the trumpet has the theme while the piano races in runs
Jerky, off-beat rhythms; piano and orchestra jab at each other
Slow and mysterious: the piano and the orchestra take turns in quiet, strange harmonies
Fast and fierce again; the piano drives hard
The theme returns in the orchestra at its first speed, while the piano runs twice as fast around it

stops.label: Last 30 seconds
stops.hear: Slow, very quiet; the piano ends on a low, soft chord
stops.happening: A quiet close in E minor

notice: Keep the opening theme in your head. In some variations it is easy to find; in others only its shape or rhythm remains.
In the final return of the theme, the orchestra and the piano play at two different speeds at once.

movements.heading: Allegro, ma non troppo
movements.summary: Prokofiev called this movement an argument between soloist and orchestra. The bassoons start a dry, stalking tune; the piano interrupts with its own ideas. A long, lyrical middle section brings a broad, romantic melody. Then the argument resumes and builds to a thrilling finish in C major.

mainIdeas.name: The argument
mainIdeas.description: a stalking tune for bassoons and [[pizzicato|pizzicato]] strings, and the piano’s interruptions.

mainIdeas.name: The lyrical theme
mainIdeas.description: a slow, yearning melody in the woodwinds, later sung by the full strings.

stops.hear: Bassoons and plucked strings play a dry, stalking tune
stops.happening: The main theme, in A minor

stops.hear: The piano cuts in with a different idea
Piano and orchestra trade blows, faster and louder, with brilliant runs and hammered chords
Everything slows down; the woodwinds play a slow, yearning melody
The piano answers with a mocking, angular version
The melody swells in the strings, broad and romantic
stops.happening: The lyrical theme at its warmest

stops.hear: Very quiet: the piano explores softly over hushed woodwinds
Piano and strings together rise to a loud climax, playing in [[unison|unison]]
stops.happening: The climax of the middle section

stops.hear: The bassoons’ stalking tune returns, and the tempo picks up
Faster and faster; the piano races in glittering double notes over the orchestra

stops.label: Last 15 seconds
stops.hear: A great, loud C major chord
stops.happening: The concerto ends in C major

notice: Listen to who starts each new section, piano or orchestra. The argument is about who leads.
The lyrical theme is the concerto’s broadest melody, almost like Rachmaninoff. Prokofiev turns it sarcastic before letting it bloom.

threads.title: Song and sparkle
threads.body: Each movement sets a singing melody (the clarinet, the gavotte, the lyrical middle section) against fast, glittering piano writing.

threads.title: A pianist’s concerto
threads.body: Prokofiev wrote it for his own technique: percussive chords, lightning runs and leaps. In 1932 he recorded it himself with the London Symphony Orchestra, his only recording of one of his own concertos.

threads.title: Ending in C major
threads.body: The concerto starts with a quiet clarinet in C major and ends with a huge C major chord for everyone.
